chunks: From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abdullah ibn Junadab, who said:

'Abbad ibn Maymun asked him (Abdullah ibn Junadab) while I was present, about a man who made a vow upon himself to fast and wanted to set out for Hajj. So Abdullah ibn Junadab said: I heard from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about a man who made a vow upon himself to fast, and then the intention for visiting Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) came upon him. He said: 'He sets out and does not fast it on the road, and when he returns, he makes up for it.'

117 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I wrote to him, the Vasi (executor), asking if he should pay the Zakat al-Fitr on behalf of orphans if they have wealth. So he wrote back (peace be upon him): 'There is no Zakat upon an orphan.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking a vow of fast while traveling for Hajj, and is Zakat al-Fitr due on orphans?
ai.summary: This chapter from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* presents two distinct juristic rulings: first, that a traveler who has vowed to fast may break their fast during the journey to Hajj or visit the Imam, making it up upon return, reflecting the Shia emphasis on balancing vows with the spiritual merit of visiting the Ahl al-Bayt; second, it clarifies that Zakat al-Fitr is not obligatory on orphans, even if they possess wealth, highlighting the exemption of dependents from direct financial obligations. These rulings illustrate the practical application of *fiqh* in managing personal vows and communal charity within the Shia tradition.
